topic: Psychological detachment from work can be practised
text:
Telling a team to switch off after hours doesn't make it happen. Research suggests switching off can be taught.

Being able to mentally detach from work in your own time is linked with lower exhaustion and better sleep, although most of that research shows links rather than cause.

A review of programs designed to improve detachment found they helped, on average. The most useful ingredients were boundaries between work and home, ways to manage emotions, and better sleep. Longer programs helped more than very short ones, and people who were already struggling with stress, rumination or sleep gained more. Benefits were still evident several months later.

The programs were tested with employees in general, not people with clinical burnout, so they are a starting point rather than a treatment.

For managers and clinicians alike: small, concrete boundary routines, such as writing tomorrow's to-do list before leaving, are an easy place to begin a conversation about recovery.

Key sources:
Karabinski, T., Haun, V. C., Nübold, A., Wendsche, J., & Wegge, J. (2021). Interventions for improving psychological detachment from work: A meta-analysis. Journal of Occupational Health Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/ocp0000280
Headrick, L., Newman, D. A., Park, Y. A., & Liang, Y. (2023). Recovery experiences for work and health outcomes: A meta-analysis and recovery-engagement-exhaustion model. Journal of Business and Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10869-022-09821-3
